The Reds | founded = {{Start date and age|1903|4|14|df=yes}} | ground = [[Pittodrie Stadium]] | capacity = 19,274{{cite web|url=https://x.com/AFCspareTickets/status/1959226531563102289|title=AFCSpareTickets|access-date=24 August 2025}} | chairman = [[Dave Cormack]] | manager = [[Stephen Robinson (footballer)|Stephen Robinson]] | league = {{Scottish football updater|Aberdeen}} | season = {{Scottish football updater|Aberdeen2}} | position = {{Scottish football updater|Aberdeen3}} | website = {{URL|https://www.afc.co.uk/|afc.co.uk}} | pattern_la1 = _aberdeen2526h | pattern_b1 = _aberdeen2526h | pattern_ra1 = _aberdeen2526h | pattern_sh1 = _aberdeen2526h | pattern_so1 = _adidasonredl | leftarm1 = fF0000 | body1 = fF0000 | rightarm1 = fF0000 | shorts1 = fF0000 | socks1 = 880000 | pattern_la2 = _aberdeen2627a | pattern_b2 = _aberdeen2627a | pattern_ra2 = _aberdeen2627a | pattern_sh2 = _aberdeen2627a | pattern_so2 = _aberdeen2627al | leftarm2 = 000029 | body2 = 000029 | rightarm2 = 000029 | shorts2 = 000029 | socks2 = 000029 | pattern_la3 = | pattern_b3 = | pattern_ra3 = | pattern_sh3 = | pattern_so3 = | leftarm3 = | body3 = | rightarm3 = | shorts3 = | socks3 = }} '''Aberdeen Football Club''' is a Scottish professional [[Association football|football]] club based in [[Aberdeen]], Scotland. They compete in the {{Scottish football updater|Aberdeen}} and have [[List of unrelegated association football clubs|never been relegated]] from the top division of the [[Scottish football league system]] since they were elected to the top flight in 1905.{{cite web |last=Nardelli |first=Alberto |title=Which European football clubs have never been relegated? |url=https://www.theguardian.com/news/datablog/2015/jun/02/which-european-football-clubs-have-never-been-relegated |quote=Only two clubs have always played in Scotland's top division: Celtic (since 1890) and Aberdeen (since 1905). |access-date=7 April 2024 |website=[[The Guardian]] |date=2 June 2015 |archive-date=7 April 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240407100141/https://www.theguardian.com/news/datablog/2015/jun/02/which-european-football-clubs-have-never-been-relegated |url-status=live}} Aberdeen have won four [[list of Scottish football champions|Scottish league titles]], eight [[Scottish Cup]]s and six [[Scottish League Cup]]s. They are also the only Scottish team to have won two European trophies, having won the [[UEFA Cup Winners' Cup|European Cup Winners' Cup]] and the [[UEFA Super Cup|European Super Cup]] in 1983. Formed in 1903 as a result of the amalgamation of three clubs from Aberdeen, they rarely challenged for honours until the post-war decade, when they won each of the major Scottish trophies under manager [[Dave Halliday]]. This level of success was surpassed in the 1980s, when, under the management of [[Alex Ferguson]], they won three league titles, four Scottish Cups and a Scottish League Cup, alongside the two European trophies. Aberdeen were the last club outside the [[Old Firm]] to win a league title, in [[1984–85 in Scottish football|1984–85]], and also the last Scottish team to win a European trophy. They have enjoyed less success since this golden era, though in the 2010s, the club ended a 19-year wait for a major trophy by winning the [[2013–14 Scottish League Cup]]; this was followed by four consecutive seasons of finishing second behind [[Celtic F.C.|Celtic]] in the league. More triumph came in 2025 as they won the [[2024–25 Scottish Cup|Scottish Cup]] for the first time in 35 years. Aberdeen have played at [[Pittodrie Stadium]] since their inception. The ground has a capacity of 19,274,{{cite web|url=https://x.com/AFCspareTickets/status/1959226531563102289|title=AFCSpareTickets|access-date=24 August 2025}} and was the first [[All-seater stadium|all-seated]] and all-covered stadium in the United Kingdom. Pittodrie was also the first football stadium to feature a [[technical area|dug-out]], an invention of player and coach [[Donald Colman]]. The club's colours have been primarily red and white since 1939; before this, they played in black and gold vertical stripes. In modern times, Aberdeen have almost exclusively played with all-red strips with white detailing.{{cite web|url=http://historicalkits.co.uk/Scottish_Football_League/Aberdeen/Aberdeen.htm|title=Aberdeen|publisher=Historical Football Kits|access-date=23 November 2017|archive-date=1 December 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171201035419/http://historicalkits.co.uk/Scottish_Football_League/Aberdeen/Aberdeen.htm|url-status=live}} Aberdeen attract support from the city and surrounding areas, as they have no geographically close rivals. Lacking a local competitor, Aberdeen have instead developed rivalries with more distant opponents such as [[Dundee United F.C.|Dundee United]] (collectively known as the "[[New Firm (Scotland)|New Firm]]" in the 1980s) and [[Rangers F.C.|Rangers]]. == History == {{main|History of Aberdeen F.C.}} {{See also|List of Aberdeen F.C. seasons}} === Formation and early years (1903–1939) === [[File:Aberdeen FC League Performance.svg|thumb|300px|alt=Chart of yearly table positions|League history of Aberdeen from their first league appearance in 1904]] Before Aberdeen FC formed, in 1902 Edinburgh based [[Hibernian F.C|Hibernian]], unsettled in the capital, were looking to move to Aberdeen, even going as far as sending a valuer to Pittodrie to decide if the move was plausible.{{cite web|url= https://www.afc.co.uk/2021/04/14/1903-aberdeen-football-amalgamation/ |title= AFC ARCHIVE ABERDEEN FOOTBALL AMALGAMATION |publisher= Red Matchday Team (Kevin Stirling) (Malcolm Panton) |access-date=11 January 2026|archive-date= 14 April 2021|archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20210414152256/https://www.afc.co.uk/2021/04/14/1903-aberdeen-football-amalgamation/|url-status=live}} This kickstarted talks of a merger between three clubs based in the city—[[Aberdeen F.C. (1881)|Aberdeen]], [[Victoria United F.C. (Scotland)|Victoria United]] and [[Orion F.C.|Orion]]—in 1903.{{sfnp|Webster|2003|pp=69–70}} The three clubs came to an agreement and the new Aberdeen FC was formed. The new club played its first match on 15 August 1903: a 1–1 draw with [[Stenhousemuir F.C.|Stenhousemuir]].{{cite web|url=http://www.afcheritage.org/history/milestones/index.cfm|title=AFC Milestones and Records|publisher=Aberdeen Heritage Trust|access-date=19 June 2016|archive-date=24 May 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160524093432/http://www.afcheritage.org/history/milestones/index.cfm|url-status=live}} That first season produced a win in the [[Aberdeenshire Cup]], but only a third-place finish in the [[Northern Football League (Scotland)|Northern League]]. The club applied for membership of the [[Scottish Football League|Scottish League]] for the following season, and were elected to the Second Division.{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=xXvlCwAAQBAJ|title=Aberdeen in 100 Dates|last=McMenemy|first=Elma|date=15 May 2016|publisher=The History Press|isbn=9780750968836|access-date=29 June 2016|archive-date=20 April 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170420033133/https://books.google.com/books?id=xXvlCwAAQBAJ|url-status=live}} In 1904, the club were managed by [[Jimmy Philip]]. At the end of its first season, despite having finished seventh out of twelve teams, Aberdeen were elected to the new, expanded First Division. They have remained in the top tier of Scottish football ever since.{{cite web |url=http://www.scotprem.premiumtv.co.uk/page/AberdeenDetail/0,,10002~932190,00.html |title=Club Overview – Aberdeen |publisher=[[Scottish Premier League]] |access-date=28 March 2008 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080411072744/http://www.scotprem.premiumtv.co.uk/page/AberdeenDetail/0%2C%2C10002~932190%2C00.html |archive-date=11 April 2008 |url-status=dead }} From 1906, the club made steady progress, with a [[Scottish Cup]] semi-final appearance in [[1907–08 in Scottish football|1908]] and another in [[1910–11 in Scottish football|1911]]. In that season of 1910–11, Aberdeen recorded their first victories over the [[Old Firm]] of [[Celtic F.C.|Celtic]] and [[Rangers F.C.|Rangers]], and led the league for a time, but finished the season in second place. Wartime affected the club as much as any other; despite spending cuts and other economies, by 1917 the situation became untenable. Aberdeen dropped out of competitive football, along with [[Dundee F.C.|Dundee]] and [[Raith Rovers F.C.|Raith Rovers]].{{sfnp|Webster|2003|pp=33}} Senior football returned on 16 August 1919, and Aberdeen resumed with a fixture against [[Albion Rovers F.C.|Albion Rovers]]. Philip was still in charge, and continued to oversee a team capable of isolated good results, but never quite able to sustain a challenge long enough to win a trophy. In 1923, Aberdeen were drawn against [[Peterhead F.C.|Peterhead]] in the Scottish Cup, and posted their record score—a 13–0 victory.{{cite news |url=http://www.highbeam.com/doc/1P2-19039673.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150924185927/http://www.highbeam.com/doc/1P2-19039673.html |url-status=usurped |archive-date=24 September 2015 |title=Peterhead ready to settle old scores with northern neighbours |work=[[Sunday Herald]] |publisher=Herald & Times Group |access-date=7 September 2013|date=4 March 2001 |last=Grant |via=[[HighBeam Research]] |url-access=subscription |first=Michael}} Philip retired a year later, and was replaced as manager by [[Paddy Travers]].{{cite web |url=https://www.soccerbase.com/managers/manager.sd?manager_id=1429 |title=Aberdeen's managers |publisher=Soccerbase |access-date=24 March 2008 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060818184825/http://www.soccerbase.com/managers2.sd?managerid=1429 |archive-date=18 August 2006 |url-status=live }} He presided over the team's first Scottish Cup final in 1937. Travers' "trainer"—first team coach in modern parlance—was former player [[Donald Colman]].{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Q2qHCwAAQBAJ|title=Team Talk: Sporting Words and their Origins|last=Walker|first=Julian|date=20 January 2013|publisher=Bloomsbury Publishing|isbn=9780747813125|access-date=29 June 2016|archive-date=20 April July 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200724205824/https://books.google.com/books?id=IdG8BQAAQBAJ|url-status=live}} [[Everton F.C.|Everton]] visited Pittodrie soon after its |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080528212721/http://www.pyramidpassion.co.uk/Text_page_scan_1.jpg |url-status=live }} Travers left to become manager of [[Clyde F.C.|Clyde]] in 1939. === Halliday to McNeill (1939–1978) === Travers was replaced by former [[Yeovil Town F.C.|Yeovil Town]] manager [[Dave Halliday]], one of more than a hundred applicants for the role, and the club moved from their black and gold strip to red and white.{{cite web|url=http://www.qosfc.com/Legends|title=Queens Legends|website=qosfc.com|publisher=[[Queen of the South F.C.|Queen of the South]]|access-date=19 June 2016|archive-date=8 July 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180708185115/http://www.qosfc.com/legends|url-status=live}}{{cite web|url=http://www.afcheritage.org/Team/Manager/index.cfm?manager_id=3|title=Dave Halliday|website=www.afcheritage.org|access-date=19 June 2016|archive-date=28 May 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150528053714/http://www.afcheritage.org/Team/Manager/index.cfm?manager_id=3|url-status=live}}{{sfnp|Miller|2011}} Halliday had barely begun his work when [[World War II]] halted competitive football in the United Kingdom. For these six years, the club was temporarily taken over by then-directors Charles B Forbes and George Anderson while Halliday served in the war.{{cite web|url=http://www.spartacus.schoolnet.co.uk/2WWfootball.htm |title=Football and the Second World War |publisher=Spartacus |access-date=28 March 2008 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080324091123/http://www.spartacus.schoolnet.co.uk/2WWfootball.htm |archive-date=24 March 2008 |url-status=usurped }} Halliday's place in the Aberdeen Hall of Fame was secured after the war when he became the first manager to bring national trophies to Pittodrie. Aberdeen won the [[Southern League Cup (Scotland)|Southern League Cup]] in the [[1945–46 in Scottish football|1945–46 season]], [[1945–46 Southern League Cup (Scotland)|defeating Rangers]] 3–2 at [[Hampden Park|Hampden]].{{Sfnp|Miller|2011}} They then reached the [[1946–47 Scottish Cup|1947 Scottish Cup]] final, defeating [[Hibernian F.C.|Hibernian]] 2–1 with [[George Hamilton (footballer)|George Hamilton]], signed from Halliday's former club [[Queen of the South F.C.|Queen of the South]], scoring to gain the club's first major trophy.{{cite web |url=http://www.tankedup-imaging.com/football/scottish.html |title=Scottish Premier League & Cup winners |publisher=Tanked Up Imaging |access-date=24 March 2008 | archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20080428005816/http://www.tankedup-imaging.com/football/scottish.html| archive-date= 28 April 2008 | url-status= live}} From this early success, Halliday's side reached two more Scottish Cup finals, in [[1952–53 in Scottish football|1953]] and [[1953–54 in Scottish football|1954]], though they lost both. Halliday's team were not to be denied, however, and the following season, [[1954–55 in Scottish football|1954–55]], Aberdeen won their first Scottish League title. Though league winners, the club did not participate in the first [[UEFA Champions League|European Cup]] competition—Scotland's place was awarded to Hibernian, who took part by special invitation.{{cite web |url=https://www.rsssf.org/ec/ec195556.html |title=European Competitions 1955/56 |access-date=29 March 2008 | archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20080315053719/http://www.rsssf.com/ec/ec195556.html| archive-date= 15 March 2008 |website=[[RSSSF]] | url-status= live}} Halliday and Hamilton left at the end of that championship-winning season, and Halliday was replaced by [[Davie Shaw]]. Aberdeen won the League Cup under his guidance, beating [[St Mirren F.C.|St Mirren]] in [[1955–56 in Scottish football|1955–56]], and reached another Scottish Cup final in [[1958–59 in Scottish football|1959]]. However, Shaw stepped aside for another former favourite player, [[Tommy Pearson]], in 1959. Pearson's time in charge coincided with a high turnover of players, and yielded no trophies.{{cite web|url=http://www.heraldscotland.com/news/12018997.Tommy_Pearson/|title=Tommy Pearson|date=6 September 1999|website=[[The Herald (Glasgow)|Herald Scotland]]|access-date=30 June 2016|archive-date=16 August 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160816053437/http://www.heraldscotland.com/news/12018997.Tommy_Pearson/|url-status=live}} He retired in 1965, making way for [[Eddie Turnbull]]. Turnbull led Aberdeen to the [[1966–67 in Scottish football|1967]] Scottish Cup final, where the side was ultimately defeated by Celtic. Despite this loss, Aberdeen qualified for the [[1967–68 European Cup Winners' Cup|European Cup Winner's Cup]] in the following season thanks to their appearance in this final, the first time the club had competed in European competition. Their first tie was a 14–1 [[Two-legged tie|aggregate]] victory over [[Knattspyrnufélag Reykjavíkur|KR Reykjavik]], although they lost the second round tie with [[Standard Liège]] 3–2 on aggregate. Two years later, [[Derek McKay|Derek "Cup-tie" McKay]] recorded the only four goals of his Aberdeen career to help his team to the [[1969–70 Scottish Cup]], scoring the winning goals in the quarter- and semi-final, and two in the final itself.{{cite web|url=http://www.dailyrecord.co.uk/news/uk-world-news/hero-footballers-where-are-they-now-967494#dRTcLLp7GwjBitdB.97|title=Hero Footballers: Where Are They Now?|last=Dow|first=Bob|date=29 January 2008|access-date=30 June 2016|archive-date=17 August 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160817171949/http://www.dailyrecord.co.uk/news/uk-world-news/hero-footballers-where-are-they-now-967494#dRTcLLp7GwjBitdB.97|url-status=live}}{{cite web|url=http://www.scotsman.com/sport/four-goal-legacy-of-cup-tie-mckay-1-1164433|title=Four-goal legacy of 'Cup-tie McKay'|date=21 April 2008|website=[[The Scotsman]]|access-date=30 June 2016|archive-date=8 May 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160508175801/http://www.scotsman.com/sport/four-goal-legacy-of-cup-tie-mckay-1-1164433|url-status=live}} As Scottish Cup holders, Aberdeen once again qualified for [[1970–71 European Cup Winners' Cup|the same competition]], but were eliminated in the first round following a 4–4 aggregate tie with [[Budapest Honvéd FC|Honvéd]]. This tie, level after extra time and also level on [[Away goals rule|away goals]], was decided by the first [[Penalty shoot-out (association football)|penalty shoot-out]] in UEFA competition history, Honvéd winning the shootout 5–4 in [[Budapest]].{{cite web|url=http://www.uefa.com/memberassociations/news/newsid=2153252.html|title=Penalty shoot-outs: the long and the short of it|last=Saffer|first=Paul|date=9 February 2015|publisher=[[UEFA]]|access-date=2 July 2016|archive-date=7 March 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160307041223/http://www.uefa.com/memberassociations/news/newsid=2153252.html|url-status=dead}}{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=__SwdvPyYN8C|title=Eddie Turnbull: Having a Ball|last1=Turnbull|first1=Eddie|last2=Hannan|first2=Martin|date=29 June 2012|publisher=Random House|isbn=9781780574684|access-date=3 September 2016|archive-date=20 April 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170420062249/https://books.google.com/books?id=__SwdvPyYN8C|url-status=live}} The Aberdeen side of the 1970s regularly challenged for domestic honours. However, they rarely won trophies, with the exception of the [[Drybrough Cup]] in 1971 under [[Jimmy Bonthrone]] and the [[1976 Scottish League Cup final|League Cup in 1976]], under [[Ally MacLeod]]. During this decade, Aberdeen had five managers: Eddie Turnbull, Jimmy Bonthrone, Ally MacLeod, [[Billy McNeill]] and [[Alex Ferguson]]. They reached two more national cup finals—the [[1978 Scottish Cup final|Scottish Cup in 1978]] under Billy McNeill and the [[1979 Scottish League Cup final (March)|League Cup in the following season]] under the new manager Alex Ferguson. === Alex Ferguson era (1978–1986) === [[File:Alex Ferguson.jpg|thumb|upright|left|alt=Photograph|[[Alex Ferguson]], the most successful manager of Aberdeen, pictured at his last club [[Manchester United F.C.|Manchester United]]]] Under Ferguson's guidance, the club won three league championships, four Scottish Cups, one League Cup, the European Cup Winner's Cup, the European Super Cup and a Drybrough Cup—all in the space of seven years.{{sfnp|Ferguson|2000}} Players such as [[Jim Leighton]], [[Willie Miller]], [[Alex McLeish]] and [[Gordon Strachan]] became the backbone of the team.{{sfnp|Webster|2003|pp=243}} Aberdeen's second League title was won in [[1979–80 in Scottish football|1979–80]] and this initial success was built upon with Scottish Cup wins in three successive seasons from [[1981–82 in Scottish football|1982]] to [[1983–84 in Scottish football|1984]], and two more league titles in 1983–84 and [[1984–85 in Scottish football|1984–85]].{{Sfnp|Ferguson|2000}}[[File:Gordon Strachan's 1983 ECWC final shirt.jpg|alt=a red football shirt showing the Aberdeen FC insignia and text showing it is from the European Cup Winners Cup final 1983|thumb|upright|Gordon Strachan's 1983 European Cup Winners Cup final shirt (on display at Spartans FC clubhouse in Edinburgh).]]During the [[1982–83 European Cup Winners' Cup|European Cup Winners' Cup in 1983]], Aberdeen beat [[FC Sion]], [[FC Dinamo City|Dinamo Tirana]] and [[Lech Poznań]] to face the [[1981–82 DFB-Pokal|German Cup]] winners [[FC Bayern Munich|Bayern Munich]]. This game was won 3–2 at Pittodrie after a goalless draw in Germany, [[John Hewitt (footballer)|John Hewitt]] with the winning goal.{{cite web|url=http://talksport.com/sir-alex-fergusons-10-greatest-european-games-manchester-united-and-aberdeen-11042623369|title=Sir Alex Ferguson's 10 greatest European games at Manchester United and Aberdeen|last=Mendes|first=Chris|date=26 April 2011|website=[[Talksport]]|access-date=29 June 2016|archive-date=21 September 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160921073411/http://talksport.com/sir-alex-fergusons-10-greatest-european-games-manchester-united-and-aberdeen-11042623369|url-status=live}}{{cite web|url=https://www.theguardian.com/football/2008/feb/15/match.newsstory|title=Uefa Cup: Aberdeen 2–2 Bayern Munich|last=Murray|first=Ewan|date=15 February 2008|website=[[The Guardian]]|access-date=29 June 2016|archive-date=13 October 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201013201153/https://www.theguardian.com/football/2008/feb/15/match.newsstory|url-status=live}} They then faced now-defunct [[Belgium|Belgian]] club [[K. Waterschei S.V. Thor Genk|Waterschei]] in the semi-final. Aberdeen beat them 5–1 at home, and lost for the first time in the tournament, 1–0 away, resulting in an aggregate victory which sent Aberdeen to the final.{{cite web|url=http://stv.tv/news/north/219028-alex-fergusons-aberdeen-maestros-thrashed-waterschei-30-years-ago/|title=The night when Bell rang the show against Belgians in Europe|website=STV News|access-date=29 June 2016|archive-date=5 August 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160805223651/http://stv.tv/news/north/219028-alex-fergusons-aberdeen-maestros-thrashed-waterschei-30-years-ago/|url-status=live}} On 11 May 1983, Aberdeen beat [[Real Madrid C.F.|Real Madrid]] 2–1 after extra time to win the cup and become only the third Scottish side to win a European trophy.{{cite web |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/scotland/sportscotland/asportingnation/article/0081/page06.shtml |title=A Sporting Nation – The New Firm and the Dons' Cup-Winners' Cup glory in 1983 |publisher=BBC |access-date=22 April 2008 |archive-date=24 October 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141024055233/http://www.bbc.co.uk/scotland/sportscotland/asportingnation/article/0081/page06.shtml |url-status=live }}{{cite news |url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/sport2/hi/sports_talk/1329596.stm |title=The greatest Euro final ever? |work=BBC News |date=16 May 2001 |access-date=30 March 2008 |archive-date=22 August 2007 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070822161757/http://news.bbc.co.uk/sport1/low/sports_talk/1329596.stm |url-status=live }} The club released a song, "European Song", to coincide with the appearance in the final.{{cite web |url=https://www.amazon.co.uk/Aberdeen-FC-Come-You-Reds/dp/B000026Y9F |title=Aberdeen FC: Come On You Reds! |publisher=[[Amazon (website)|Amazon]] |access-date=20 April 2008| archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20080601093722/http://www.amazon.co.uk/Aberdeen-FC-Come-You-Reds/dp/B000026Y9F| archive-date= 1 June 2008 | url-status= live}} This was followed up with the capture of the [[UEFA Super Cup|European Super Cup]] in December, when [[Hamburger SV]] were beaten over two legs.{{cite news|url=https://www.theguardian.com/football/that-1980s-sports-blog/2016/mar/09/aberdeen-scottish-football-alex-ferguson|title=When Aberdeen ruled Scottish football|date=9 March 2016|access-date=20 April 2017|work=[[The Guardian]]|archive-date=20 April 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170420102017/https://www.theguardian.com/football/that-1980s-sports-blog/2016/mar/09/aberdeen-scottish-football-alex-ferguson|url-status=live}} Aberdeen reached the semi-finals of the [[1983–84 European Cup Winners' Cup]], before losing to [[FC Porto|Porto]] 2–0 on aggregate. (1881)|Aberdeen]] club, but lasted only one season before being replaced.{{Cite web |date=26 June 2017 |title=The history of the blue kit |url=https://www.afc.co.uk/2017/06/26/the-history-of-the-blue-kit/ |access-date=7 January 2024 |publisher=Aberdeen F.C. |language=en |archive-date=18 February 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190218022804/https://www.afc.co.uk/2017/06/26/the-history-of-the-blue-kit/ |url-status=live }} For the [[1904–05 in Scottish football|1904–05]] season, Aberdeen adopted a black and gold striped shirt, which led to the team being nicknamed "the Wasps".{{cite web|url=http://www.afcheritage.org/Team/Manager/index.cfm?manager_id=1|title=Aberdeen Football Club Managers|website=www.afcheritage.org|access-date=2 June 2016|archive-date=28 May 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150528060306/http://www.afcheritage.org/Team/Manager/index.cfm?manager_id=1|url-status=live}} This strip, with only minor variations, was worn until just before the start of the Second World War. The blue shorts lasted until 1911, and then were replaced with white ones. Socks were black with gold trim, either as stripes or as a solid bar at the turndown. {{Football kit box |align = left |pattern_la = |pattern_b = |pattern_ra = |leftarm = E41B17 |body = E41B17 |rightarm = E41B17 |shorts = FFFFFF |socks = E41B17 |title = A representative post-war Aberdeen strip. These colours were worn for all the trophy-winning seasons of the 1950s. }} In March 1939, Aberdeen changed the black and gold colours to red and white, reflecting the silver and red colours of the official City of Aberdeen arms. The first red strips were worn with white shorts, with either red or white socks from 1939 until the [[1965–66 in Scottish football|1965–66]] season. In 1966, Aberdeen adopted red shorts, making the official kit all-red, similar to that of [[Liverpool F.C.|Liverpool]], who made a similar change at around the same time.{{cite web |url=http://www.historicalkits.co.uk/Liverpool/Liverpool.htm |title=Liverpool|publisher=Historical Football Kits |access-date=8 January 2008 | archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20071217225529/http://www.historicalkits.co.uk/Liverpool/Liverpool.htm| archive-date= 17 December 2007 | url-status= live}} This arrangement has continued to the present day, with several variations in design, in common with most senior clubs as the replica shirt market has expanded.{{Cite news|url=https://www.theguardian.com/money/blog/2010/sep/21/football-kits-premier-league-cash-cow|title=Football kits: Premier League teams turn style into a cash cow|last=Khan|first=Mehreen|date=21 September 2010|newspaper=The Guardian|issn=0261-3077|access-date=12 November 2016|archive-date=13 November 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161113042846/https://www.theguardian.com/money/blog/2010/sep/21/football-kits-premier-league-cash-cow|url-status=live}} In the late 1970s an [[Admiral Sportswear|Admiral]] strip featured five vertical white stripes on the left side of the shirt and shorts, and the early 1980s shirts—as worn at the 1983 European Cup Winners Cup final—featured white vertical pinstripes. The club did not have an official crest before 1972, but several variations on the letters AFC had from time to time featured on the shirt, usually in some kind of [[cursive]] font. In November 1972,{{cite web | url=http://www.footballcrests.com/clubs/aberdeen-fc | title=Aberdeen | work=Football Crests.com | access-date=19 August 2007 | archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20070824163451/http://www.footballcrests.com/clubs/aberdeen-fc| archive-date= 24 August 2007 | url-status= live}} the club unveiled an official crest or logo, designed by Aberdonian graphic designer Donald Addison. The design represented a capital letter ''A'' as the side view of a football goal, with a ball forming the crossbar of the letter. This ball was crosshatched in such a way as to depict it as being inside the net, signifying the scoring of a goal. The logo was completed by the letters ''FC'' in smaller type at a level with the ball element. This badge was used on the shirts from around 1978, with no significant alterations until the mid-1980s when the words "Aberdeen Football Club" were added in a circular border, and the date of the club's founding, 1903, was added under the goal element. The current version of the crest, which retains these elements in a unified design, was introduced at the start of the [[1997–98 in Scottish football|1997–98]] season.
